paragraphs: He stood behind the pulpit with confidence, voice steady, Bible open, people listening. He spoke about holiness. About obedience. About surrender. But there was something you couldn’t ignore, something that kept pressing against your conscience no matter how polished his sermons sounded.
You knew.
He had multiple wives.
Not in the past. Not before Christ.
Now.
And he wasn’t hiding it.
But here’s what most people don’t realize… truth is not measured by how powerful someone sounds, but by how faithfully they submit to the Word of God when no one is clapping.
Because Scripture doesn’t stay silent about the life of a leader.
“Now the overseer is to be above reproach, faithful to his wife…” (1 Timothy 3:2)
Read that again.
Above reproach.
Faithful to his wife.
Not wives.
God saw it.
And you felt the tension. Because part of you wants to say, “But he preaches so well.” Another part whispers, “But something is off.” And that whisper matters more than the applause around him.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

This is where many people get trapped. They separate the message from the messenger, as if a man can live in ongoing disobedience and still be trusted to rightly divide the truth. But Scripture doesn’t make that separation when it comes to leadership.
It raises the standard.
Not lowers it.
“Not many of you should become teachers… because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.” (James 3:1)
More strictly.
Not less.
So what does it mean when a preacher continually practices polygamy, not in ignorance, not in confusion, but in ongoing, unrepentant lifestyle?
It reveals something deeper than cultural difference.
It reveals rebellion.
You don’t accidentally live in contradiction to God’s design for marriage while claiming to shepherd His people. From the beginning, God defined it clearly:
“A man shall leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)
One.
Not divided.
Not multiplied.
Jesus Himself reaffirmed it:
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” (Matthew 19:6)
You cannot stretch “one flesh” into multiple covenants without distorting what God established.
And here’s where it becomes personal.
Because this isn’t just about him.
It’s about you.
Why are you still listening?
Is it because his words make you feel something? Because his delivery is compelling? Because confronting the truth would cost you comfort, community, maybe even identity?
You knew.

There’s a quiet compromise that happens when we sit under teaching that contradicts Scripture. Not overnight. Not loudly. But slowly. Your sensitivity dulls. Your discernment weakens. And eventually, what once troubled you becomes something you defend.
That’s dangerous.
Because Jesus didn’t say, “Follow whoever speaks well.”
He said, “My sheep hear My voice… and they follow Me.” (John 10:27)
His voice.
Not charisma.
Not influence.
Not popularity.
So can you trust a preacher who continually practices polygamy?
Not if you take Scripture seriously.
Not if you believe God’s standard matters.
Not if you understand that leadership in the Kingdom is not about gifting, but about surrender.
Because the real issue is not just his lifestyle.
It’s his refusal to repent.
And that’s where the Gospel confronts everything.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
Yes, even him.
Yes, even you.
But the difference between a man called by God and a man building his own platform is not perfection.
It’s repentance.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just and will forgive us…” (1 John 1:9)
Forgiveness is available.
Grace is real.
But grace does not excuse ongoing rebellion.
It transforms it.
This is the line many refuse to cross. They want grace without surrender. Influence without accountability. Authority without obedience.
But Jesus didn’t die to affirm your sin.
He died to free you from it.
And that includes leaders.
So now you’re faced with something you can’t ignore anymore.
Two paths.
You keep listening, adjusting your convictions to fit his life.
Or you step away, align yourself with truth, even if it costs you something.
One leads to slow compromise.
The other leads to life.
Say it plainly: “Truth over comfort.” Let that be your line.
Someone else needs to hear this too. You know exactly who. Send it to them.
Because conviction fades if you don’t revisit it.
And if you’re ready to go deeper, to grow in discernment, to be sharpened in truth instead of confused by culture, there’s more waiting for you.
